articles.title: In 1997, a horse jumped a fence and joined one of Franceâs prestigious cycling races; it ran through the peloton and reached the front before leaving 20 kilometres from the finish
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In March 1997, amidst the professional cyclists of the CritÃ©rium International, a horse jumped onto the course, raced with the peloton, and became an unforgettable and chaotic part of the race's history.
articles.body: In March 1997, the CritÃ©rium International peloton suddenly gained an unexpected companion: a horse. The animal had jumped a fence beside the course and landed directly in the path of the fast-moving cyclists. Rather than turning away, it ran alongside the riders, moved through the group and eventually reached the front. The interruption became one of the most memorable moments in the history of the race.According to Cyclingnews, the incident took place on March 29, 1997, during the opening stage of the CritÃ©rium International, a French stage race held in the Tarn region that year. The 188-kilometre stage ran from Blaye-les-Mines to Rabastens and featured riders such as Laurent Jalabert, Marco Pantani and Chris Boardman. Late in the race, a horse escaped from a field and joined the peloton, creating confusion among the riders. The animal remained with the group for several kilometres before falling away and disappearing from the race, with reports placing the incident roughly 15 to 20 kilometres from the finish.When the peloton met a runaway horseThe riders were travelling together when the horse suddenly cleared a fence bordering the road. Television footage captured the animal landing on the course and immediately joining the stream of cyclists. For the riders, the appearance was more than a curiosity; it was a serious hazard. A horse running at speed in the middle of a tightly packed peloton could easily have caused a serious crash. FrÃ©dÃ©ric Moncassin later recalled the dramatic sound of the animal landing, describing the noise of its hooves, the sparks and its breathing. The horse, however, did not panic. It continued forward with the cyclists.Rather than remaining behind the pack, the animal began moving through it. It passed riders and worked its way towards the front, creating an extraordinary scene in which a four-legged intruder appeared to be competing against some of Europe's best professional cyclists. The horse eventually reached the front of the group and crossed the bridge at Lisle-sur-Tarn ahead of the riders. When the cyclists approached a junction, the race turned while the horse continued straight ahead, finally leaving the course and ending its unexpected appearance in the race.The race continued without its unexpected challengerThe horse may have been the most memorable part of the opening stage, but the race continued and produced a very different story over the following two stages. In the first stage, StÃ©phane Barthe of Casino won the 188-kilometre route from Blaye-les-Mines to Rabastens in a sprint, finishing ahead of Mario Traversoni and FrÃ©dÃ©ric Moncassin. His victory gave him the early overall lead, while the horse that had briefly joined the peloton became an unusual footnote to the day's racing.The Cyclenews also notes that the following morning overall standings changed during the mountain stage to Pic de Nore. Marcelino GarcÃ­a of ONCE attacked on the final climb of the 80-kilometre stage and finished about a minute ahead of Laurent Jalabert and the other leading riders. The result put GarcÃ­a into the overall lead. The race then concluded that afternoon with an eight-kilometre individual time trial in Castres. GarcÃ­a did not need to win the stage to secure the title. His ONCE teammate Aitor Garmendia recorded the fastest time, ahead of Chris Boardman, while GarcÃ­a finished sixth and protected his lead. He went on to win the 1997 CritÃ©rium International overall, leaving the horse as the unlikely star of the race's opening day.From cycling footage to film historyWhat began as a bizarre moment during a professional cycling race did not remain confined to the world of sport. Footage of the horse running alongside the peloton was later used in AmÃ©lie, the 2001 French film directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, giving the incident a second life on screen. The horse had appeared during the opening stage of the 1997 CritÃ©rium International, a long-running French stage race that attracted many of the sport's leading riders and was often part of their preparation for bigger races later in the season.What made the footage so striking was not simply that a horse had wandered onto the course. The animal moved alongside the peloton for several kilometres, keeping pace with the riders as they continued the stage. For a brief stretch, the professional race took on an unusual appearance, with the cyclists following their race tactics while an unexpected horse travelled among them.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners
articles.summary: The US has threatened to isolate nations that continue to do business with Tehran, which sells much of its oil to Beijing.
articles.body:
China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.

Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.

Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."

Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.

He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".

However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".

The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.

"We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".

Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions

The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.

It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war.

The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade.

Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement.

With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".

UK Chancellor John Healey said the British government supported "US work to secure a diplomatic solution and welcome efforts to increase pressure".

Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further.

He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.

But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response.

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.

This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate."

And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people.

Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.

articles.title: âJailed or killedâ: How Iran is silencing citizens as internal tensions mount
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran is tightening its grip on citizens as internal tensions mount, introducing tougher restrictions on communication with foreign media and instituti.
articles.body: Iran is tightening its grip on citizens as internal tensions mount, introducing tougher restrictions on communication with foreign media and institutions amid growing fears of dissent. The latest measures come as the country faces mounting economic pressure, with US sanctions threatening further disruption while the Iranian rial has fallen to a record low, worsening pressure on ordinary Iranians.According to Newsnationâs report, citing NewsNation and regime-monitored Iranian media, Tehran has introduced new regulations criminalising contact with what it describes as âhostileâ media outlets. A bill titled âCountering the Infiltration of Intelligence Services and Foreign Governments or Institutions in the Countryâ reportedly makes interviews with foreign media an offence, specifically naming US and Israeli outlets. Those found sharing information could face up to two years in prison.The measures extend beyond media interactions, with academic cooperation and communication with foreign institutions also potentially coming under scrutiny. An Iranian refugee who spoke to NewsNation anonymously for safety said the rules were designed to prevent Iranians from informing the outside world about abuses and organising future protests.âThese new rules are another attempt by the regime to tighten its control over people and prevent any form of independent connection or cooperation with the outside world,â the refugee said.âThis goes far beyond ordinary regulation or censorship. It is about controlling who people are allowed to communicate and cooperate with, particularly when those connections could expose them to ideas, opportunities, information, or networks outside the regimeâs control,â they added.US sanctions deepen economic pressureThe crackdown comes as Iran faces intensified economic pressure from Washington. The US has announced expanded sanctions targeting Tehran and warned that countries continuing to trade with Iran could also face secondary sanctions. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei warned that Tehran would respond to any escalation, saying, âOur hands are not tied.âThe pressure is being felt inside Iran, where the currency has hit a record low. While the Iranian economy has adapted to years of sanctions by developing domestic industries and finding alternative trading partners, further restrictions risk pushing up the cost of basic goods and deepening public frustration.Iranian refugee Rayan Amiri, founding leader of the Conservative Party of Iran, said the latest measures reflected a broader strategy of ruling through fear. âThe Islamist regime is afraid that these voices may receive international attention and inform the international community about the dreadful and Orwellian situation in Iran,â Amiri said.He alleged that the regime labels activists and commentators as CIA or Mossad agents and seeks to imprison or assassinate critics abroad. He cited the killings of Iranian exiles Masoud Molavi and Saeed Karimian in Turkey as examples.The crackdown has also extended to people sharing information about unrest. Earlier this month, the Islamic Republicâs judiciary warned that anyone sharing footage or information with âhostile states against national security and interestsâ that causes âpublic panicâ could face the capital charge of âCorruption on Earthâ.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Suffolk Wildlife Trust launches 'first-of-its-kind' nature survey
articles.summary: A wildlife group says "everyone can get involved with protecting nature" by taking part in research.
articles.body:
A wildlife trust has said it has launched a first-of-its-kind survey to help find out how people feel about nature and guide future conservation efforts.

The Suffolk Wildlife Trust (SWT), in collaboration with the University of Suffolk, has brought out the Great Suffolk Nature Survey, which quizzes participants on the county's "struggling" wildlife.

It asks about their experiences with local wildlife, how they get involved with local nature, and their attitudes towards conservation, climate change and environmental projects.

The short survey comes weeks after a devastating wildfire at Dunwich Heath and nearby RSPB Minsmere destroyed vital wildlife habitats, which could take years to recover.

Jack Cripps, head of marketing and communications at SWT, said: "The county's landscapes and wildlife are a huge part of what I and so many others who live here are proud of.

"But our wildlife is struggling and we're really starting to feel the impacts of our changing climate. This survey will go a bit deeper into what local people think and feel about nature.

"Everyone can get involved with protecting nature, and the results of the survey will guide Suffolk Wildlife Trust's future community projects and campaigning."

This is the first time SWT has run its own survey, although it has previously gathered local responses as part of the nationwide The Great Big Nature Survey.

Hannah Page, from the University of Suffolk, said it was "delighted" to be supporting the trust with the "important project".

She also said there would be an opportunity for a student from the university to help roll out the survey thanks to a paid student placement from the county council.

Jack Cripps, head of marketing and communications at SWT, said: "The county's landscapes and wildlife are a huge part of what I and so many others who live here are proud of.
"But our wildlife is struggling and we're really starting to feel the impacts of our changing climate. This survey will go a bit deeper into what local people think and feel about nature.
"Everyone can get involved with protecting nature, and the results of the survey will guide Suffolk Wildlife Trust's future community projects and campaigning."
This is the first time SWT has run its own survey, although it has previously gathered local responses as part of the nationwide The Great Big Nature Survey.
Hannah Page, from the University of Suffolk, said it was "delighted" to be supporting the trust with the "important project".
She also said there would be an opportunity for a student from the university to help roll out the survey thanks to a paid student placement from the county council.

articles.title: Trump says Strait of Hormuz has been demined, warns Iran not to plant more
articles.summary: Aug 25 (Reuters) - U.S.
articles.body:
Aug 25 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that all mines ‌had been detonated or removed from international ‌waters of the Strait of Hormuz and that Iran ​has been told that any ship or boat placing new mines will be destroyed.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the United ‌States, through its ⁠Space Force, was watching "every square inch" of the Strait, a key waterway ⁠in the global energy supply chain.

"There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in ​full ​force and effect," Trump ​said.

The U.S. and ‌Iran have not conducted air strikes on each other's militaries for weeks, but attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued as the two sides vie for control ‌of the narrow maritime passage.

Oil ​transits through the strait ​were at 5 ​million barrels per day on ‌Monday, provisional data from shiptracker ​Vortexa showed, ​down from more than 20 million per day before the war or about one ​of every ‌five barrels consumed worldwide.

(Reporting by Daphne Psaledakis ​and Ismail Shakil; editing by Michelle ​Nichols and Katharine Jackson)

articles.title: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
articles.summary: Flight tracking data confirms an American military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday.
articles.body:
The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.

John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet.

In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.

Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. It departed later on Tuesday.

BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment.

Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.

It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in the Russian capital at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24. It returned to Riga shortly before 17:00 GMT.

Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow.

Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.

The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow.

John Foreman, who served as a British military attachÃ© to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme that the visit could be focused on "escalation management" given speculation recent drone activity in Germany could be linked to Russia .

He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."

Foreman said the trip could also concern the release of US detainees currently being held in Russia.

Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine.

The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.

The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.

Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.

Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.

Additional reporting by Washington correspondent Daniel Bush and BBC Verify

articles.title: European Court of Human Rights orders Turkey to free Osman Kavala
articles.summary: Philanthropist and activist Osman Kavala has spent almost a decade in jail over charges rights groups say are politically motivated.
articles.body:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has ordered Turkey to immediately release Osman Kavala, an activist and philanthropist who has been detained in prison for almost a decade.

Kavala was sentenced to life behind bars in 2022 for charges related to nationwide protests in 2013 and a failed coup attempt three years later.

Since his initial arrest and detention in 2017, rights groups and Kavala himself have maintained that the charges against him are politically motivated.

The ECHR on Tuesday ruled that his continued detention was unlawful and that his rights to a fair trial, freedom of expression and association had been violated.

"The measures taken against the applicant... had been predominantly motivated by an ulterior purpose, namely, to punish him for his role in the Gezi Park demonstrations and for expressing his opinions as a human rights defender, and to silence him," the court said in its ruling , external .

The court also found that Kavala's aggravated life sentence amounted to "inhuman and degrading treatment".

Rights advocates and opposition groups say President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government has increasingly weaponised the judiciary to target critics and rivals.

The court said Kavala's case had exposed a "systemic problem" in Turkey of the "detention and prosecution of political opponents, human rights defenders and journalists", adding that there were "structural shortcomings which affected the guarantees of independence and impartiality of the judiciary".

The Turkish government has insisted the country's courts are independent.

Turkish activist sentenced to life in prison Published 26 April 2022

Turkish activist sentenced to life in prison

The case that set Turkey on collision course with the West Published 25 November 2021

The case that set Turkey on collision course with the West

Kavala, 68, became a symbol of a government crackdown on civil society in Turkey following his arrest in October 2017.

He and others were accused of orchestrating and financing anti-government protests in 2013, which started in Istanbul's Gezi park before spreading across Turkey.

The demonstrations posed the first serious challenge to the rule of Erdogan, who was Turkey's dominant prime minister at the time and became its directly elected president the following year.

Human rights group Amnesty International says prosecutors falsely alleged that the Gezi park protests were an attempt to overthrow the government.

In 2019, the ECHR demanded Kavala's immediate release, describing his detention as arbitrary and politically motivated. Turkey did not implement the ruling.

He was initially acquitted in February 2020 but within hours was rearrested on new charges of being part of a failed military coup in 2016.

His acquittal over the Gezi Park protests was overturned in January 2021, and he was sentenced to life in prison in April 2022 - a conviction now declared "null and void" by the ECHR.

Reacting to the latest ECHR ruling, Amnesty International's Eve Geddie said: "This obstruction of justice must end. Turkey's authorities, including judicial and prosecutorial, must act to free Osman Kavala immediately and unconditionally."

Kavala was born in Paris and educated in the UK. Before being thrust to prominence, he ran a cultural centre.

Erdogan has previously accused Kavala of being an agent of the Hungarian-born US billionaire George Soros.

Turkey has refused to comply with the two previous ECHR rulings on Kavala's case, and it is not clear whether Ankara will implement the court's third binding ruling.

The case remains one of the most serious recent flashpoints between Ankara and Strasbourg.

The Council of Europe oversees how its 46 member states execute ECHR rulings. It has the power to freeze a country's membership or suspend its voting rights if it is found to have seriously violated the rule of law.

Even though Turkey has failed to comply with several key ECHR decisions, it remains a founding member, engages with the system and has not broken ties.

A meeting of the Committee of Ministers in mid-September is likely to prioritise the Kavala case, but it remains to be seen whether it will debate harsh punitive measures.

articles.title: Nigeria's president orders manhunt after kidnappers upload victim video
articles.summary: The footage shows dozens of men, women and children sitting in a forest.
articles.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who launched deadly attacks on four villages in a remote part of Niger state last Friday.

Local residents told the BBC several mosques were simultaneously targeted during prayers. A local youth leader says as many as 500 people may have been abducted, though this has not been verified.

The president's orders came after the kidnappers posted a video on social media of what they said were those abducted last week sitting in a forest.

The authorities had previously suspected the attackers were bandits - criminal gangs involved in kidnapping and looting for ransom across parts of Nigeria.

The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria

The gunmen, reportedly dressed in military-style clothing, attacked the villages of Dekara, Gidan Zana, Sabon Gida and Masaka.

Police spokesman Wasiu Abiodun told the BBC that more than 40 people were killed, but the exact number of deaths had not been confirmed.

Looking at the footage released on social media, the local youth leader, who asked not to be named, said he recognised several individuals from his community.

"I was able to identify many people. There is an elderly man in the video who is like a grandfather to us," he said. "He lives in Gidan Zana village."

He said families who had spotted relatives in the video were relieved to know they were still alive.

"At least they know where their loved ones are and hope they may be rescued, unlike those who still have no information about missing relatives," he added.

A local blogger familiar with the area told the BBC that many residents had fled their homes, seeking refuge in neighbouring states or across the border in Benin.

Some survivors are receiving hospital treatment, including people with serious injuries.

A local official also told the BBC that the attackers planted improvised explosive devices in parts of the affected communities as they led abductees into the forest. He said a teenage boy was killed when an explosive detonated as he tried to escape.

In a statement issued by presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga, Tinubu condemned the killings and abductions and vowed that those responsible would be brought to justice.

"Those who carried out this cowardly attack on defenceless Nigerians are enemies of peace and enemies of humanity, who will not go scot-free," the statement said.

The president also expressed his condolences to the families of those killed.

The attack is the latest sign of worsening insecurity in the Borgu area, which borders Kebbi and Kwara states as well as neighbouring Benin.

Earlier this month, police said 145 people had been rescued after being abducted from four other villages in the area.

Local officials have also raised concerns about the growing presence of jihadist groups operating in parts of north-western Nigeria and along the border region, saying some fighters have recently entered communities and imposed religious restrictions on residents.

articles.title: 'Shocking' book about Putin's private life wins French literary prize
articles.summary: A taboo-breaking book about Vladimir Putin's rise to power and private life, written by two exiled Russian journalists, won a newly established French litera...
articles.body:
A taboo-breaking book about Vladimir Putin's rise to power and private life, written by two exiled Russian journalists, won a newly established French literary prize on Tuesday.

The book, titled "The Tsar in Propria Persona: How Vladimir Putin Deceived Us All", draws on more than two decades of investigative reporting by journalists Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin.

The work won a newly established literary award called the Prix Strasbourg awarded by EBRA, France's largest regional newspaper group, and its parent company, Credit Mutuel Alliance Federale.

The book is due to be published in France next month.

It reads "like a spy novel", the jury said, describing the book as a "fascinating and shocking work about a figure who is himself fascinating and shocking".

"It is the result of several hundred interviews with witnesses, some of whom later disappeared under tragic circumstances."

Badanin is the founder and editor-in-chief of Proekt, an investigative media outlet created in 2018.

Both Badanin and Rubin, his deputy at Proekt, live in the United States after coming under pressure in Russia.

Badanin said the authors wanted foreigners to read the book and learn "actual facts" about Putin and the system he had built.

"The message we wanted to convey with this book is as follows: there is no need to invent anything about Putin. Instead, learn how things really are. That is horrifying enough," he told AFP.

"Only a genuine understanding of the facts can help us make sound assessments, respond effectively, and plan for the future of relations between nations."

When the book's Russian edition was published last year, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) said that Badanin and Rubin broke a Kremlin-imposed taboo about Putin's private life "at great personal risk".

The book "contrasts the official image of the Russian president, now in his 26th year in power, as a leading defender of traditional values against Western decadence with the reality of his private life -- where extramarital affairs, nepotism, and connections to organised crime reign".

Launched in 2026, the prize seeks to distinguish itself through its substantial endowment, with 20,000 euros ($23,000) awarded to the overall winner and 55,000 euros distributed across all categories.

Other prize winners include Haitian author Thelyson Orelien and French journalist Marion Dubreuil.

articles.title: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis
articles.summary: Several thousand migrants remain in the enclave after a mass crossing from Morocco in late July.
articles.body:
The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

"I want to apologise to all those who may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared for," Defence Minister Margarita Robles told a parliamentary committee.

"I have witnessed first-hand your feelings of anxiety, of abandonment, of lack of safety."

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa on 30 and 31 July.

Most of the migrants swam around the border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor, Juan JesÃºs Vivas.

The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most sleeping rough on beaches or streets.

articles.title: More than 50 kidnapped after violent gang attack in Haiti leaves 47 dead
articles.summary: It is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in Haiti in recent years, and one gang leader is threatening to kill the hostages.
articles.body: PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti — At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped after armed men attacked a once-peaceful community near Haiti’s capital earlier this week, the United Nations said Tuesday. It is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in Haiti in recent years, and one gang leader is threatening to kill the hostages if authorities kill any gang members as they try to secure the community nestled in the hills above Port-au-Prince. Sunday’s attack on Kenscoff pierced the belief that security in the troubled Caribbean country was improving. “This is a major political and security test, for the government, for the police and for the international mission alike,” said Romain Le Cour, head of Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. He said the threat of executing hostages is a trap: If forces don’t act, they’ve failed to protect them; if they do and hostages die, the gangs will blame the state. A threat posted on social media In a video posted on social media, the gang leader threatened Vladimir Paraison, director of Haiti’s National Police. “Paraison, if any of our soldiers are hurt, I will kill all of them,” he said, referring to the hostages. The gang member identified himself as Izo 2, a reference to Izo, or Johnson André, one of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders. Le Cour said Izo 2 is also known as “Didi” and leads the armed group in Kenscoff on behalf of and in coordination with Izo and other gang leaders. He said the aim of Sunday’s attack could be to force Haiti’s police and the U.N.-backed gang suppression force to disperse even more of their limited resources. “They don’t have enough personnel,” Le Cour said in a phone interview. “If you force them to deploy more troops, it would inevitably be at the expense of other areas.” The attack might also just be a show of force and a message to Haiti’s government and police as the country prepares to hold general elections on Dec. 13 for the first time in more than a decade. “This is a message to the government and the police that their claims of protection do not match reality,” Le Cour said. “The gangs are saying: When we choose to attack, we can, and we will succeed.” Attacks on Kenscoff have escalated The first major attack on Kenscoff occurred in January 2025, and since then, there have been sporadic attacks in the mountains surrounding the city center. But Sunday’s attack was the largest yet. At least five of the 47 people killed were children, according to the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti, known as BINUH. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack on Tuesday, noting that 22 of the victims were reportedly executed in a church compound where they had sought shelter: “The relentless gang attacks on communities and the loss of lives underscore the alarming security conditions in Haiti.” Kenscoff Mayor Jean Massillon told The Associated Press on Tuesday that gangs set fire to 25 homes and killed two government employees, including his cousin, who served as his security detail. “The atrocity of this crime reminds us that we have to continue working stronger every day to bring peace to the community,” Massillon said. “I’m optimistic that the state will continue working to eradicate the gangs in Kenscoff.” Gangs are coveting Kenscoff because it allows them to surround and control the upscale community of Pétion-Ville and alternate routes connecting Haiti’s capital to its southern region, said María Fernanda Arocha, a researcher with the nonprofit Armed Conflict Location & Event Data. Between January and August this year, security operations had managed to reduce violence in Kenscoff by 66% prior to the attack, she said in a statement. “While security forces have concentrated their efforts on operations aimed at regaining control in the central areas of Port-au-Prince, criminal groups have instead sought to expand into rural communities that are vulnerable due to the limited response capacity of the police, but which remain strategic hubs,” she added. Haitians demand police protection Some survivors accused the government of not providing enough protection prior to the attack, with Haiti’s National Police rejecting those accusations. Le Cour said that if police and armored vehicles were indeed stationed in Kenscoff prior to the attack, then the assertion is concerning: “You let the gangs come in even if you had everything in place?” Armed men control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swaths of land in Haiti’s central region and beyond. Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June and another 1,400 injured, according to U.N. statistics released Tuesday. The U.N. noted that nearly 800 rapes were reported from April to June, with 87% of those cases representing collective rapes. At least 81 people also were reported kidnapped during that time period, according to a new U.N. report. “These figures represent only a portion of the total number of people kidnapped,” it stated. “In many cases, victims’ relatives do not report kidnappings to the police or service providers and choose to negotiate directly with the kidnappers, believing that this approach allows for a quicker release and avoids possible reprisals.” The number of kidnappings reported from April to June represents a more than 40% increase compared with the previous quarter.

articles.title: Massive fishing boat runs aground at popular beach with 1,000 gallons of diesel on board
articles.summary: A 58-foot fishing boat ran aground at North Beach in Northern California's Point Reyes National Seashore, triggering a closure and diesel removal effort.
articles.body: A 58-foot fishing boat ran aground at a popular Northern California beach — prompting a closure as crews worked to remove roughly 1,000 gallons of diesel from the vessel. The Lake Bay became stranded early Friday at North Beach in Point Reyes National Seashore, according to an alert from the National Park Service (NPS). The boat was carrying 40,000 pounds of squid at the time, Inverness resident Richard James told the Point Reyes Light, a local newspaper, citing a conversation with the vessel's skipper. TSUNAMI OF SEWAGE FROM MEXICO BARRELS TOWARD US COASTLINE, OFFICIALS WARN As crews began responding to the grounding, the park service announced the temporary closing of North Beach and North Beach Road. No injuries, fuel leaks or impacts to wildlife were reported, the agency said. Fox News Digital reached out to the NPS for further comment and details. The Lake Bay can hold up to 2,800 gallons of fuel. It was reported to have approximately 1,000 gallons of diesel on board, according to a press release from the U.S. Coast Guard. Crews were coordinating with the party responsible for the vessel and a contracted salvage company to remove the fuel, the Coast Guard said. 75-FOOT BOAT SURFS WAVE, RUNS AGROUND IN HAWAII Capt. Jack Moran, owner of Sea Tow Cape May in New Jersey, told Fox News Digital that access and timing can pose challenges when dealing with a grounded vessel.  "The biggest thing is going to be accessibility," Moran said, noting that crews have to contend with tides, currents and changing conditions. "Time is the enemy. You want to try and get it off there as quickly as possible." (He is not connected to or involved with the Lake Bay fishing boat.)  With 40,000 pounds of squid reportedly onboard, Moran said removing the catch could present another challenge. "Moving a product like that is challenging at a dock, let alone removing squid from a boat on a beach," he said. For the Coast Guard, safety and environmental concerns remained at the center of the response. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Our top priorities are ensuring the safety of the first responders and the public, stabilizing the incident, and limiting environmental impacts," Lt. Cmdr. Carey Lewis, the Coast Guard incident commander, said in the release.  "Responders are continuously monitoring and evaluating the site for pollution and any potential risk factors so we can approach operations with [an] intention to minimize environmental impacts." "Our top priorities are ensuring the safety of the first responders and the public." The National Park Service asked visitors to stay away from North Beach while the closure is in effect to allow first responders to work safely. The cause of the grounding remains under investigation, the Coast Guard said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Fox News Digital previously reported on another grounding in April involving a small cruise ship near Monuriki Island in Fiji, where the Tom Hanks movie "Cast Away" was filmed. The Blue Lagoon Cruises vessel struck a reef after worsening weather caused its anchor to drag. A high-speed ferry arrived around dawn to assist with the evacuation, allowing all passengers and non-essential crew members to leave the stranded ship with their belongings. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Passengers were taken back to Port Denarau, where the cruise line arranged hotel accommodations and alternative activities. No injuries were reported among passengers or crew. Jessica Mekles of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

articles.title: Seven killed in Gaza as Israeli strike ‘destroys’ aid supply warehouse
articles.summary: Health Ministry warns of ‘complete collapse of the basic necessities of life’ in Gaza as Israel’s attacks continue.
articles.body:
Israeli strikes have killed at least seven Palestinians across Gaza, according to local medical sources, in ongoing violations of a "ceasefire" that went into effect last October.

Three Palestinians were killed and others injured in a strike on a home in Beit Lahiya, near Kamal Adwan Hospital, on Tuesday, a source at al-Shifa Hospital said.

Earlier in the day, a drone strike that hit a gathering of civilians killed a man in Khan Younis's al-Mawasi area, and injured three others.

Three other Palestinians died from wounds they sustained in earlier Israeli raids on Khan Younis, said Al Jazeera Arabic correspondent Nour Khaled.

Two of them died from injuries suffered in an attack on Monday, while the third had been wounded about two weeks ago, she said.

An Israeli military strike overnight into Tuesday also destroyed a warehouse storing nutrition supplies intended for children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers in Gaza, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) said.

"The force of the explosion caused large sections of the building to collapse, including the roof and walls, completely burying supplies beneath the rubble," MAP said in a statement.

"Humanitarian workers, humanitarian facilities and the supplies that people depend on must be protected," it added.

The warehouse belongs to Ard El Insan (AEI), a local humanitarian organisation working with MAP to support about 60 medical points serving up to 100 women and children daily.

The overnight explosion collapsed large sections of the building, including the roof and walls, burying the supplies under rubble, according to MAP, which said the entire stock was damaged and rendered unfit for human consumption.

"Losing these quantities in their entirety is a major blow to our work and will undoubtedly affect our ability to reach the children and women who need these services, particularly given the conditions they continue to face in the aftermath of starvation," said Sahar Salem, AEI's project coordinator.

"Even with the ceasefire, conditions on the ground remain extremely challenging, and children and women still urgently need continued support, she added.

She said two of her colleagues have been killed and another wounded since Israel's genocidal war on Gaza began.

Also on Tuesday, the head of Gaza's Ministry of Health warned of "complete collapse of the basic necessities of life" amid critical oxygen supply shortages.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Director-General Dr Munir al-Bursh said that Israel "continues to escalate its attacks on Gaza and violate the ceasefire agreement, which is present in statements but absent from people's lives on the ground".

Al-Bursh added that "only 12 oxygen stations remain operational out of around 34", and warned that "any additional breakdown could cut off oxygen to patients".

"If this oxygen supply stops, these people will die," he said. "We do not want to reach the point where a doctor is forced to choose between two patients, deciding who receives oxygen and who is left without it."

Ongoing Israeli attacks and ceasefire violations come despite US President Donald Trump's call for Israel to halt its attacks.

In an interview with Fox News on August 17, Trump said that Israel "should not be striking in Gaza", and that "Hamas agreed to lay down their weapons" under the terms of a US-backed peace plan.

articles.title: Prominent Sikh separatist says FBI has warned him of new threat on his life
articles.summary: A prominent Sikh separatist said Tuesday that the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have warned him that he faces a new credible threat to his life e...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — A prominent Sikh separatist said Tuesday that the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have warned him that he faces a new credible threat to his life even as a man from India faces sentencing later this year for a 2023 death plot against him.

Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, general counsel for Sikhs For Justice, said he was warned by FBI agents who visited him last Thursday that he should not travel until the threat is resolved, and, if he does, the agency should be notified in advance of his plans.

He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police warned him by telephone on Tuesday, though neither law enforcement agency gave any details about the plot that was uncovered. Messages seeking comment from both law enforcement agencies were not immediately returned.

Pannun, a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen, said he was warned according to the terms of a "Duty to Warn" law in the United States that obligates U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies to notify individuals when they discover credible and specific threats of murder, severe bodily harm or kidnapping.

The new threat comes as Nikhil Gupta, a man from India who pleaded guilty to federal conspiracy charges in February, awaits a Nov. 20 sentencing in Manhattan federal court for plotting in 2023 with others to assassinate Pannun.

The FBI has said Gupta was directed by an Indian government employee to carry out the killing. When Gupta tried, he unwittingly communicated with an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman. Federal sentencing guidelines call for Gupta to spend at least two decades in prison.

Pannun, who advocates for the creation of the sovereign Sikh state and is considered a terrorist by the Indian government, said in a phone interview Tuesday that he was "unfazed and undaunted" by the attempts to silence him.

"I'm not afraid of their death threats," he said, though he added that he hoped that the administrations of President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney would confront Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi over threats to U.S. and Canadian sovereignty.

"The Modi government is proceeding under the Trump administration without fear of any consequences," he said.

Pannun has described himself as a Sikh human rights lawyer who is campaigning to turn Punjab into a place where "all religions will have equal rights."

He said "Duty to Warn" advisories were issued by Canadian law enforcement officials to Hardeep Singh Nijjar, the ex-head of the Canadian chapter of the Khalistan Referendum, in the weeks before he was assassinated on June 18, 2023 in Surrey, British Columbia.

Pannun said the continued threats give him courage and confidence that his campaign and outspokenness is working.

"I'm going to continue, even at the cost of a bullet," he said.
paragraphs: NEW YORK (AP) — A prominent Sikh separatist said Tuesday that the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have warned him that he faces a new credible threat to his life even as a man from India faces sentencing later this year for a 2023 death plot against him.

Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, general counsel for Sikhs For Justice, said he was warned by FBI agents who visited him last Thursday that he should not travel until the threat is resolved, and, if he does, the agency should be notified in advance of his plans.

He said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police warned him by telephone on Tuesday, though neither law enforcement agency gave any details about the plot that was uncovered. Messages seeking comment from both law enforcement agencies were not immediately returned.

Pannun, a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen, said he was warned according to the terms of a "Duty to Warn" law in the United States that obligates U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies to notify individuals when they discover credible and specific threats of murder, severe bodily harm or kidnapping.

The new threat comes as Nikhil Gupta, a man from India who pleaded guilty to federal conspiracy charges in February, awaits a Nov. 20 sentencing in Manhattan federal court for plotting in 2023 with others to assassinate Pannun.

The FBI has said Gupta was directed by an Indian government employee to carry out the killing. When Gupta tried, he unwittingly communicated with an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman. Federal sentencing guidelines call for Gupta to spend at least two decades in prison.

Pannun, who advocates for the creation of the sovereign Sikh state and is considered a terrorist by the Indian government, said in a phone interview Tuesday that he was "unfazed and undaunted" by the attempts to silence him.

"I'm not afraid of their death threats," he said, though he added that he hoped that the administrations of President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney would confront Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi over threats to U.S. and Canadian sovereignty.
"The Modi government is proceeding under the Trump administration without fear of any consequences," he said.
Pannun has described himself as a Sikh human rights lawyer who is campaigning to turn Punjab into a place where "all religions will have equal rights."

He said "Duty to Warn" advisories were issued by Canadian law enforcement officials to Hardeep Singh Nijjar, the ex-head of the Canadian chapter of the Khalistan Referendum, in the weeks before he was assassinated on June 18, 2023 in Surrey, British Columbia.
Pannun said the continued threats give him courage and confidence that his campaign and outspokenness is working.
"I'm going to continue, even at the cost of a bullet," he said.

articles.title: Yamaha Awards Over $225,000 in Q2 2026 Access Grants
articles.summary: Let's get the kids back outside!
articles.body:
Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative Awards Over $225,000 in Q2 2026 Grants

Funding Supports Youth Outdoor Education, Trail Stewardship, and Responsible Motorized Recreation

MARIETTA, Ga. – August 25, 2026 – Yamaha Motor Corp., USA, awarded more than $225,000 in second-quarter funding through the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative (Yamaha OAI), supporting seven organizations working to expand responsible access to outdoor and motorized recreation through youth education, trail stewardship, ride area safety improvements, and enhanced access opportunities.

The latest grants fund projects ranging from youth boating, fishing, and bicycling education to trail rehabilitation, new trail development, improved wayfinding, and track and riding-area safety. The quarter also brings together Yamaha OAI and Yamaha Rightwaters to help expand outdoor recreation opportunities for young people through boating and fishing programs on California's Catalina Island.

"This quarter's recipients demonstrate the many ways responsible recreation and long-term outdoor access go hand-in-hand, from introducing young people to lifelong outdoor activities to maintaining the trails and riding areas enthusiasts depend on," said Steve Nessl, Yamaha Motorsports marketing director. "We're also proud to continue our support of All Kids Bike for a fifth year, helping give kindergarteners at more than 50 elementary schools nationwide the opportunity to learn how to ride a bike through their physical education programs."

Q2 2026 Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative Grant Recipients

Yamaha OAI awarded grants to the following organizations during the second-quarter funding cycle:

Catalina Outdoor Adventure Club (RJ Nautical, Avalon, Calif.) received funding, along with a 40-horsepower outboard motor contributed by Yamaha Rightwaters, to expand youth boating and fishing programs on Catalina Island.

GARTRA – Georgia Recreational Trail Riders Association (Nelson Powersports, Blue Ridge, Ga.) received funding to support trail maintenance at seven OHV areas throughout Georgia.

Quad Cities ATV Club (Five Seasons Sports, Eveleth, Minn.) will rehabilitate two heavily used trails that connect riders to a regional trail system in northern Minnesota.

San Luis Valley Great Outdoors (Peak Motor Sports, Alamosa, Colo.) will develop a new connector trail and improve wayfinding signage in Colorado's San Luis Valley.

Strider Education Foundation / All Kids Bike will expand its Kindergarten PE Learn-to-Ride Program to 12 additional schools nationwide, continuing a partnership with Yamaha OAI that began in 2021.

Summit County Off-Road Riders (SCORR) (Silverthorne Powersports, Silverthorne, Colo.) will make track maintenance and safety improvements at its motocross facility in Dillon, Colorado.

West Central Montana Avalanche Foundation (Five Valley Honda Yamaha, Missoula, Mont.) will support backcountry trail maintenance and safety education for motorized recreation in the Seeley Lake region.

Yamaha OAI accepts applications year-round and awards grants quarterly to eligible organizations working to improve access to outdoor recreation. The program prioritizes projects that promote safe and responsible motorized recreation, maintain and improve trails and riding areas, and help protect sustainable access to public lands.

The application deadline for Q3 2026 grants is September 30, 2026. Public land managers, riding clubs, land stewardship organizations, and outdoor recreation groups are encouraged to learn more and apply at YamahaOAI.com.

Follow Yamaha Outdoors on social media at @YamahaOutdoors and share your adventures using #Yamaha, #YamahaOAI, #REALizeYourAdventure, and #ProvenOffRoad.

About the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative

Since 2008, the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative has led the powersports industry in supporting responsible access to our nation's public lands for outdoor enthusiasts. With more than $8 million contributed to over 575 projects across the country, Yamaha has directly and indirectly supported thousands of miles of motorized recreation trails, maintained and rehabilitated riding and hunting areas, improved staging areas, supplied organizations with essential OHV safety education, built bridges over fish-bearing streams, helped children learn to ride bicycles, and partnered with local outdoor enthusiast communities to improve access to public lands. Each quarter, Yamaha accepts applications from nonprofit or tax-exempt organizations, including OHV riding and cycling clubs and associations, national, state, and local public land-use agencies, outdoor enthusiast associations, and land conservation groups with an interest in protecting, improving, expanding, and/or maintaining access for safe, responsible, and sustainable public use.

For updated guidelines, the application form, and the latest Outdoor Access Initiative news, please visit YamahaOAI.com. If you have specific inquiries about the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative, you can reach the dedicated hotline at 1-877-OHV-TRAIL (877-648-8724), email OHVAccess@Yamaha-Motor.com, or send correspondence to:

Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative 3065 Chastain Meadows Parkway, Bldg. 100 Marietta, GA 30066

articles.title: Train Operator Appears Asleep Moments Before Rear-Ending Another Train
articles.summary: A newly released video appears to show a San Francisco Muni operator asleep moments before his light rail train strikes the rear of another train. The impact...
articles.body:
A newly released video appears to show a San Francisco Muni operator asleep moments before his light rail train strikes the rear of another train. The impact jolts the operator forward and shatters the front window of his cab.

The collision happened shortly after 8:30 a.m. on July 31 near 47th Avenue and Wawona Street in San Francisco's Outer Parkside neighborhood. Both vehicles were operating on the L Taraval line, according to ABC7 News .

Although early accounts described both trains as empty, the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA) later told local news outlets that two passengers were aboard one of the moving trains. They exited after the crash, and no injuries were reported.

SFMTA verified the video and initially attributed the collision to operator error caused by fatigue. Its formal investigation remains underway.

Video Shows the Operator Nod off for About 20 Seconds

Embedded media follows. Please allow a moment for it to load.

The onboard footage shows the operator scratching his head before his hand drops and his head begins to lower. He appears to remain asleep for approximately 20 seconds as the train continues along Wawona Street, KTVU reported.

The operator then wakes, looks ahead and appears to brace himself after seeing the stopped train in front of him. The collision throws him forward as broken glass falls into the cab.

SFMTA Ruled Out Equipment and Track Problems

SFMTA said its initial review found no vehicle or infrastructure failure that would explain the crash. The agency instead identified fatigue-related operator error as the preliminary cause.

The operator was moved to non-driving duties while SFMTA completes its investigation with the California Public Utilities Commission. The agency has not announced when that investigation will conclude or how fast the train was traveling before impact.

SFMTA told NBC Bay Area that it has increased random video reviews and added rest time to operator shifts in response to fatigue concerns.

Another Operator Fatigue Incident Happened Last Year

A separate Muni operator appeared to fall asleep aboard a crowded N Judah train on Sept. 24, 2025. That train accelerated to approximately 50 mph while leaving the Sunset Tunnel, throwing some passengers from their seats.

SFMTA also attributed the incident to operator fatigue after ruling out mechanical failure. The agency placed that operator on non-driving status and launched a fatigue-awareness campaign for employees. SFMTA has since provided operators with additional safety training and bulletins about fatigue resources.
